sections.h: 'Truly' against 'in appearance': Ignatius to the Trallians 9-10
sections.b: Lightfoot: the letter's 'main purport ... is a warning against the poison of Docetism', and 'The denunciation of Docetism is fuller and more explicit in this than in any other of his letters'. Ignatius quotes the claim, 'he suffered only in appearance', and turns it back: 'they themselves are only in appearance!' (Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1). Against it he sets a confession with 'truly' four times: Christ 'was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified and died ... He was also truly raised from the dead' (Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2). His last argument is his own chains: if Christ's suffering was a show, 'Then I am dying for nothing' (Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1). The teachers mix Christ into their teaching 'to win trust', like poison 'mixed with honeyed wine' (Ignatius to the Trallians 6:2). Whether they also kept Jewish practices is 'disputed' (Lake); Lightfoot thinks they did.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 6:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1; 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 1:7

common: Docetism was the teaching that Christ only seemed to have a human body and to suffer.

claude.title: Claude's theory: why 'he ate and drank'
claude.body: Ignatius puts 'he ate and drank' between 'truly born' and 'truly persecuted' (Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1). A teacher who said Christ only seemed to have a body could grant his preaching and miracles, but eating is a body's need. The same point is made of the risen Christ in Luke 24:42-43 and Acts 10:41. Lightfoot's paraphrase draws out the same point ('His human body was no mere phantom ... He really ate and drank'); I suggest further that Ignatius chose the most ordinary act he could, to leave the teachers no room.
claude.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1; Luke 24:42-43; Acts 10:41; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 3:3

sections.h: Of David's family and of Mary: Ignatius to the Trallians 9
sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2 confesses Jesus Christ 'of David's family and of Mary', 'truly born', eating and drinking, persecuted under Pontius Pilate, crucified, dead 'in the sight of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth', and 'truly raised from the dead' by his Father, who 'will also raise us who believe in him'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2; Romans 1:3; Galatians 4:4; Philippians 2:10

sections.h: Overseer, elders and deacons at Tralles
sections.b: Tralles sent only its overseer, Polybius, to Ignatius (Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1); Eusebius calls him the church's 'ruler then' (Church History 3.36.5). The letter asks the church to be subject to the overseer 'as to Jesus Christ' and to the elders 'as to the apostles of Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Trallians 2:1-2), to respect the overseer as 'a type of the Father' and the elders 'as God's council and as the band of the apostles': 'Without these, it is not called a church' (Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1). The elders above all are to 'refresh the overseer' (Ignatius to the Trallians 12:2). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 3:1 at 1549 and 1554.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 2:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 7:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 13:2

sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians 2:3 calls the deacons 'deacons of the mysteries of Jesus Christ' who 'must please everyone in every way': 'For they are not deacons of food and drink, but assistants of the church of God.' In 3:1 they are to be respected 'as Jesus Christ'. Against Acts 6:2, where the Seven are chosen 'to serve tables', the letter shows the deacon's office as more than serving food.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 2:3; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1; Acts 6:1-6; 1 Corinthians 4:1

sections.h: 'Without these it is not called a church'
sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1 ends its list of overseer, elders and deacons with 'Without these, it is not called a church'. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it (Catechism 1554). The Lutheran and Baptist confessions do not discuss Ignatius, but answer the question in their own words: the Augsburg Confession (VII) defines the church as 'the congregation of saints, in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the Sacraments are rightly administered', and the Second London Baptist Confession (26.8) names a church's officers as 'bishops or elders, and deacons'. The same letter pictures the church as branches of the cross and as members joined to their head: 'a head cannot be born apart, without members, since God promises union, which is himself' (Ignatius to the Trallians 11:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 7:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 11:2; Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 12:12

sections.h: The elders 'as the apostles' in Trallians
sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians 2:2 asks the church to be subject to the council of elders 'as to the apostles of Jesus Christ', and 3:1 calls the elders 'the band of the apostles'. As in Ignatius to the Magnesians 6:1, the elders stand for the apostles; the letter does not speak of a succession from them.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 2:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 7:1

sections.b: In Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1 Pilate's name stands in the confession: 'He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate.'

Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1 confesses Christ 'of David's family and of Mary', and 'truly born'. Here Ignatius names her as his real human mother; he speaks of her virginity in Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1 and of the birth 'of a virgin' in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1.

sections.h: The Father raised him, and will raise us
sections.b: 'He was also truly raised from the dead, when his Father raised him. In the same way his Father will also raise us who believe in him, in Christ Jesus, without whom we do not have true life' (Ignatius to the Trallians 9:2). Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 15:12 and following.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 9:2; 1 Corinthians 15:12-20; Romans 8:11

sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians 11:2 pictures the cross as a tree whose branches are the true believers, with fruit that does not decay: 'If they were, they would show themselves as branches of the cross, and their fruit would be incorruptible.'
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 11:1-2; John 15:5; Acts 5:30

sections.h: The foreign weed and the poisoned wine
sections.b: Ignatius to the Trallians calls heresy 'the foreign weed' (Ignatius to the Trallians 6:1), its teachers poisoners who give 'a deadly poison mixed with honeyed wine' (Ignatius to the Trallians 6:2) and 'bad offshoots that bear deadly fruit' who 'are not the Father's planting' (Ignatius to the Trallians 11:1), echoing Matthew 15:13. Yet Ignatius writes that he does not know of 'anything of this kind among you' (Ignatius to the Trallians 8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 6:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 8:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 11:1; Matthew 15:13

sections.b: Ignatius claims to understand 'heavenly things, the places of the angels and the gatherings of the rulers, seen and unseen', but says it does not make him a disciple (Ignatius to the Trallians 5:2), with Colossians 1:16 in Lake's margin.

In Ignatius to the Trallians 5:2 the heavenly powers have 'places' and 'gatherings' (systaseis; Lightfoot: 'the assemblages, musterings, of the heavenly rulers'), 'seen and unseen'; in 4:2 'the ruler of this age is brought down' by gentleness.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 4:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 5:2; Colossians 1:16; Ephesians 6:12

sections.h: The ruler of this age and the devil's snares
sections.b: Ignatius needs gentleness, 'by which the ruler of this age is brought down' (Ignatius to the Trallians 4:2), and warns of 'the snares of the devil' (Ignatius to the Trallians 8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 4:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 8:1

sections.b: Ignatius asks, 'Why do I even pray to fight wild beasts?' (Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1), with Paul's verb from 1 Corinthians 15:32, and asks prayer that he may not be found 'disqualified' (Ignatius to the Trallians 12:3; 1 Corinthians 9:27).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:3; 1 Corinthians 15:32

sections.b: 'I greet you from Smyrna, together with the churches of God that are here with me' (Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1); 'The love of the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians greets you' (Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1

sections.b: 'Remember in your prayers the church in Syria. I am not worthy to be called one of its people, since I am the last of them' (Ignatius to the Trallians 13:1).

Written from Smyrna (Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1) after the overseer of Tralles, Polybius, visited him (Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1). It holds the much-quoted 'Without these, it is not called a church' (Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1) and the fullest of Ignatius's attacks on the teaching that Christ suffered 'only in appearance' (Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-10:1, as Lightfoot says).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 1:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 3:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 9:1-2; Ignatius to the Trallians 10:1; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:1

sections.b: Ignatius writes 'I do love to suffer, but I do not know if I am worthy' (Ignatius to the Trallians 4:2), asks prayer that he may reach his lot and 'not be found disqualified' (Ignatius to the Trallians 12:3), and says 'My spirit gives itself as an offering for you, not only now but also when I reach God' (Ignatius to the Trallians 13:3).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Trallians 4:2; Ignatius to the Trallians 12:3; Ignatius to the Trallians 13:3
